sections.title: How does the Oblique triangle calculator work?
sections.html:
The Oblique triangle calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports angle α (SSS results) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the given); then you type in the side a (SSS inputs), the side b (SSS inputs), the side c (SSS inputs) and the side a (SAS inputs).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: The formula behind the Oblique triangle calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Angle α=(((1 ÷ 2) × (-(side a ^ 2) + (side b ^ 2) + (side c ^ 2)) ÷ (side b × side c)))
Angle ß=(((1 ÷ 2) × ((side a ^ 2) − (side b ^ 2) + (side c ^ 2)) ÷ (side a × side c)))
Angle γ=(((1 ÷ 2) × ((side a ^ 2) + (side b ^ 2) − (side c ^ 2)) ÷ (side a × side b)))
S 1=((1 ÷ 2) × side a + (1 ÷ 2) × side b + (1 ÷ 2) × side c)
Area=(the square root of ((-side a × side b × side c + side a × side b × ((1 ÷ 2) × side a + (1 ÷ 2) × side b + (1 ÷ 2) × side c) + side a × side c × ((1 ÷ 2) × side a + (1 ÷ 2) × side b + (1 ÷ 2) × side c) − side a × (((1 ÷ 2) × side a + (1 ÷ 2) × side b + (1 ÷ 2) × side c), 2) + side b × side c × ((1 ÷ 2) × side a + (1 ÷ 2) × side b + (1 ÷ 2) × side c) − side b × (((1 ÷ 2) × side a + (1 ÷ 2) × side b + (1 ÷ 2) × side c), 2) − side c × (((1 ÷ 2) × side a + (1 ÷ 2) × side b + (1 ÷ 2) × side c), 2) + (((1 ÷ 2) × side a + (1 ÷ 2) × side b + (1 ÷ 2) × side c), 3)) × ((1 ÷ 2) × side a + (1 ÷ 2) × side b + (1 ÷ 2) × side c)))
Side c=(the square root of ((side a ^ 2) − 2 × side a × side b × the cosine of (angle γ) + (side b ^ 2)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Oblique triangle calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the side a and the side b — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Oblique triangle calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns angle α (SSS results), derived from the side a and the side b. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Oblique triangle calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the side a and the side b, which is 13 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter side a (SSS inputs) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Side a (SSS inputs) opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Oblique triangle calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
